steps.user_message: Here's my situation for 2024 taxes. I'm single, live in San Diego CA. My employer Midwest Health Systems paid me $84,900 (W-2). I also earned $8,900 doing consulting for 3 clients, got $920 interest from Marcus savings account and $195 dividends from E*TRADE. I work from home in a 100 sq ft office; rent is $2,100/month, total space 690 sq ft. I paid $4,800 in student loan interest (MOHELA, 2016–2019), gave $720 to Doctors Without Borders I have the receipt, and had $780 in work supplies. What's deductible? Standard or itemize? How do I handle the home office? What forms or worksheets?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Thanks — very clear. I’ll first give the short answers, then show the numbers and the exact forms/worksheets you’ll use and what I’ll need if you want me to run the math for you.

Short answers (quick):
- Deductible for federal tax: your consulting business expenses (supplies), the home‑office deduction (only for the self‑employment portion), half of your self‑employment tax (an adjustment to income), and potentially up to $2,500 of student‑loan interest (subject to income phase‑outs). The $720 charitable gift is deductible only if you itemize.
- Standard vs itemize: Most likely take the standard deduction unless you have significant other itemizable deductions (mortgage interest, large state income/property taxes, large medical expenses). With only $720 in charitable gifts shown, itemizing is unlikely to beat the standard deduction.
- Home office: Because you have consulting income (self‑employment), you can claim a home‑office deduction for the space used exclusively for your consulting work; employees generally cannot. You can use either the simplified method ($5/sq ft up to 300 sq ft) or the regular/actual‑expense method (use Form 8829). Choose the method that gives the larger allowable deduction (actual must be reported on Form 8829; simplified is claimed directly on Schedule C).
- Key forms/worksheets: Schedule C (profit/loss from self‑employment), Schedule SE (self‑employment tax), Form 8829 (home office — only for actual expense method), Form 1040 Schedule 1 (student loan interest adjustment), Form 8995 (or 8995‑A) for the Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction if applicable, and possibly Schedule B if interest/dividends exceed $1,500 (your totals are below that).

Estimated calculations (showing both home‑office methods)
Inputs you gave:
- W‑2 wages: $84,900
- Consulting gross: $8,900
- Interest: $920
- Dividends: $195
- Business supplies: $780
- Home office: 100 sq ft; total home = 690 sq ft → office portion = 100/690 ≈ 14.49%
- Rent: $2,100/month → $25,200/year
- Student loan interest paid: $4,800 (see clarifying Q below)
- Charitable cash: $720

1) Self‑employment net and SE tax (before home office)
- Gross consulting: $8,900
- Less supplies: $780
- = $8,120 (net before home office)

A. If you use the simplified home‑office method ($5/sq ft):
- Home office deduction = 100 sq ft × $5 = $500
- Schedule C net profit = 8,900 − 780 − 500 = $7,620
- Self‑employment tax: compute on 92.35% of net: 7,620 × 0.9235 ≈ 7,039 → SE tax ≈ 7,039 × 0.153 ≈ $1,077
- Half of SE tax (above‑the‑line deduction) ≈ $538

B. If you use the actual (pro rata) method and allocate rent only (you can also allocate utilities, renter’s insurance, etc., if you have them):
- Home office portion of rent = $25,200 × 14.49% ≈ $3,651
- Schedule C net profit = 8,900 − 780 − 3,651 = $4,469
- SE tax: 4,469 × 0.9235 ≈ 4,127 → SE tax ≈ 4,127 × 0.153 ≈ $632
- Half of SE tax ≈ $316

So the actual method gives a much larger home‑office deduction (and reduces taxable self‑employment income more), but must be documented and reported on Form 8829. Note: home‑office deduction cannot exceed your business gross income minus other business expenses — in your case both methods produce a positive profit, so you’re fine.

2) Student‑loan interest deduction
- The maximum student‑loan interest deduction is $2,500 (subject to MAGI phaseouts and eligibility). You cannot deduct more than that.
- Whether you can take the deduction (and whether it’s the full $2,500) depends on your modified adjusted gross income (MAGI). Rough AGI estimate (before the student‑loan adjustment) with each home‑office method:

  - Using simplified method estimate:
    AGI ≈ W‑2 (84,900) + interest/dividends (1,115) + net SE (7,620) − half SE tax (≈538) ≈ 92,097

  - Using actual method estimate:
    AGI ≈ 84,900 + 1,115 + 4,469 − 316 ≈ 90,168

Given those ballpark AGIs, you may be at or above the published phaseout range for the student loan interest deduction for single filers — which means the deduction may be reduced or eliminated. You’ll need your exact MAGI and the 1098‑E from MOHELA to determine the exact allowable amount. (If your MAGI is under the lower phaseout limit you can take up to $2,500; if it’s above the upper limit you get none; if in between it’s prorated.)

3) Charitable contributions
- Only deductible if you itemize. With only $720 in charitable gifts shown (and no other big itemizable items provided), you’ll most likely be better off taking the standard deduction.

4) Interest & dividends reporting
- Report the $920 interest and $195 dividends on your Form 1040. Schedule B is only required if total interest + dividends > $1,500 (yours = $1,115 → no Schedule B required).

5) QBI (Section 199A)
- Because you have self‑employment income, you may be eligible for the 20% Qualified Business Income deduction on (a portion of) your Schedule C net income. With small net income from the business the QBI amount will be small. Form 8995 (simpler) or 8995‑A (if thresholds/limitations apply) is used to claim it.

6) Estimated taxes / withholding
- You’ll owe self‑employment tax on your net Schedule C profit; you’ll also pay income tax on that net profit. Because you have substantial W‑2 wages, your employer withholding may cover most of your income tax, but you may still owe SE tax (and possibly some additional income tax). If you haven’t made estimated payments and your withholding is insufficient you could owe estimated taxes/penalties. Check pay stubs and total withholding to see if estimated payments are needed.

Forms and worksheets you’ll use (federal):
- Form 1040
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — report consulting income and supplies, and the home‑office deduction if simplified (if actual, see below)
- Schedule SE (Self‑Employment Tax)
- Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) — use only if using the actual/regular method for home office
- Form 8995 or 8995‑A (QBI deduction), if applicable
- Schedule 1 (additional adjustments) — student loan interest deduction is reported here
- Schedule B only if interest+dividends > $1,500 (not needed here)
- Keep Form 1099‑NEC(s) (if clients issued them), Form 1098‑E (student loan interest), 1099‑INT, 1099‑DIV, and W‑2

Documentation to keep:
- Receipts for supplies ($780), charity receipt for Doctors Without Borders ($720), records proving the home office (floor plan, photos, date put into use, rent/utility statements), Form 1098‑E or loan statements showing interest paid, 1099s, and W‑2.

Recommendations / next steps I can do for you
- If you want, I can run the exact numbers for you (taxable income estimate and approximate federal tax due) — I’ll need:
  - Confirmation that the $4,800 interest was paid in tax year 2024 and whether you have a 1098‑E
  - Any state/local taxes paid (state tax withheld or estimated tax paid) and any mortgage interest/property taxes (if any)
  - Any other itemizable expenses (large medical, property tax, SALT amounts)
  - Whether your clients issued 1099‑NEC forms
  - Any utilities or other home expenses you want to include for the actual home‑office method (utilities, renter’s insurance, internet portion, etc.)
- If you prefer, use the simplified home‑office method (easier record‑keeping, less IRS formwork) or the actual method (likely larger deduction in your case because of high rent) — I can compute which yields the bigger tax savings.

One important tax note
- Home office deductions are only allowed for the self‑employment business portion of your work. If you are doing consulting as an independent contractor (Schedule C), the home office is allowable. If you tried to claim home office for your W‑2 employment (and your employer did not reimburse you), federal law generally disallows that deduction.

Would you like me to run the full estimated tax calculation (approx. federal tax and self‑employment tax) using the actual home‑office method vs the simplified method? If so, please confirm:
- Was the $4,800 interest paid in 2024 and do you have Form 1098‑E?
- Any state income tax or property tax amounts withheld/paid in 2024?
- Any utilities/insurance amounts for the home to include in the actual home‑office method?
